title: Ensure sshd PermitEmptyPasswords is disabled
description: The recommendation is to edit the /etc/ssh/sshd_config file to ensure that the SSH daemon does not authenticate users with a null password. If password authentication is used and an account has an empty password, the SSH server must be configured to disallow access to the account. Permitting empty passwords could create an easy path of access for hackers to enter the system. Audit: evaluates the effective configuration from `sshd -T` (Match blocks must be reviewed separately).
reference: CIS IBM AIX 7 Benchmark v1.2.0 - 4.6.3.13 Ensure sshd PermitEmptyPasswords is disabled

audit.command: command -v sshd >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1; out=$(sshd -T 2>/dev/null) || exit 1; r=compliant; for p in '^permitemptypasswords[[:blank:]]+no$'; do printf '%s\n' "$out" | grep -Eiq -- "$p" || r="not matched: $p"; done; echo "$r"

remediation.guidance: Edit the /etc/ssh/sshd_config file to disable the acceptance null passwords: vi /etc/ssh/sshd_config Replace: #PermitEmptyPasswords no With: PermitEmptyPasswords no Re-cycle the sshd daemon to pick up the configuration changes: stopsrc -s sshd startsrc -s sshd

title: Ensure Trusted Execution Path is enabled
description: The recommendation is to activate TE to enhance system integrity by specifying authorized locations for applications to hamper attacks from unauthorized locations using Trojan horse style tactics. TE provides a robust system integrity checking process. Hackers utilize any opening they can find to infiltrate a system. One common attack pattern includes getting an unauthorized program (aka Trojan horse) installed anywhere on the target system. Audit: trustchk -p TE TEP must report TE=ON and TEP=ON (review the TEP path list manually).
reference: CIS IBM AIX 7 Benchmark v1.2.0 - 2.2 Ensure Trusted Execution Path is enabled

audit.command: command -v trustchk >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1; out=$(trustchk -p TE TEP 2>/dev/null) || exit 1; r=compliant; for p in '^TE=ON$' '^TEP=ON$'; do printf '%s\n' "$out" | grep -Eq -- "$p" || r="missing: $p"; done; echo "$r"

remediation.command: NOTE: Your configuration of TE is dependent on the unique requirements of your environment. To configure TE to enforce a Trusted Execution Path (TEP) you need to know the intended secure path. e.g., SecurePath="/usr/bin:/usr/sbin" Perform the following: # First disable both TE and TEP trustchk -p TE=OFF TEP=OFF # Set the secure TEP variable trustchk -p TEP=${SecurePath} # Enable TE and TEP trustchk -p TE=ON TEP=ON Further details regarding planning and implementation of TE can be found within the IBM AIX 7 Infocentre: https://www.ibm.com/docs/en/aix/7.3?topic=configuration-trusted-execution

title: Ensure Trusted Execution (TE) policies are locked
description: Set trusted execution policy LOCK_KERN_POLICIES to enabled. All of the other policies will then be locked and cannot be changed without disabling the LOCK_KERN_POLICIES policy and then restarting the system. When policies are locked, unauthorized users cannot make changes to the policies to allow them to execute unapproved tools and then revert the settings afterwards. An unplanned system reboot is likely to be noticed and investigated Audit: automated read-only check derived from the CIS audit procedure; it prints "compliant" when the control is met.
reference: CIS IBM AIX 7 Benchmark v1.2.0 - 2.3 Ensure Trusted Execution (TE) policies are locked

audit.command: command -v trustchk >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1; out=$(trustchk -p LOCK_KERN_POLICIES 2>/dev/null) || exit 1; r=compliant; for p in '^LOCK_KERN_POLICIES=ON$'; do printf '%s\n' "$out" | grep -Eq -- "$p" || r="missing: $p"; done; echo "$r"

remediation.command: Execute the following command trustchk -p LOCK_KERN_POLICIES=ON

title: Ensure Unauthorized Applications are reported
description: At Level 1, utilize Trusted Execution (TE) to log execution of applications not yet allowlisted. This can be used to update the allowlist (TSD - /etc/security/tsd/tsd.dat) so that, at Profile Level 2, non-listed applications are actually prevented from executing. Trusted Execution (TE) provides an additional layer of access controls to processes on top of the base Discretionary Access Controls. Monitoring how processes access system resources can improve awareness of system integrity. Audit: automated read-only check derived from the CIS audit procedure; it prints "compliant" when the control is met.
reference: CIS IBM AIX 7 Benchmark v1.2.0 - 2.4 Ensure Unauthorized Applications are reported

audit.command: command -v trustchk >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1; out=$(trustchk -p TE CHKEXEC 2>/dev/null) || exit 1; r=compliant; for p in "^TE=ON$" "^CHKEXEC=ON$"; do printf '%s\n' "$out" | grep -Eq "$p" || r="missing $p"; done; grep -Eq "^[[:blank:]]*kern\.info[[:blank:]]" /etc/syslog.conf 2>/dev/null || r="kern.info not collected in /etc/syslog.conf"; echo "$r"

remediation.command: 1. Run the following command: # /usr/sbin/trustchk -p TE=ON CHKEXEC=ON 2. If logging for kern.info events is not already configured: Run the following commands: # /usr/bin/mkdir -p /var/log/syslog # /usr/bin/touch /var/log/syslog/kernel.log # print "kern.info /var/log/syslog/kernel.log rotate time 1d files 30 compress" >> /etc/syslog.conf # /usr/bin/refresh -s syslogd || /usr/bin/startsrc -s syslogd Note: Log retention periods should be configured as per site policy.

title: Ensure regular scans for unauthorized applications
description: This recommendation is find and report (audit) software on the system that has not been included in the TE (trusted execution) TSD (trusted signature database). These entries establish a so-called AllowList. Software not included on this AllowList should be generating a syslog and/or audit record whenever it is executed.
reference: CIS IBM AIX 7 Benchmark v1.2.0 - 2.6 Ensure regular scans for unauthorized applications

audit.command: The following command will locate the software AIX considers untrusted aka TROJAN. Note: the output goes to stderr so stderr is first joined to stdout and thereafter stdout get redirected to /dev/null. The argument -i instructs the scan to ignore NFS mounts. trustchk -i -n tree / 2>&1 >/dev/null | grep untrusted

remediation.command: This will be a manual process. The remediation is to find and remove the offending file (currently the reported file might be the artifact of another error - most common is a symbolic link that points at a non-existent object). The starting point is running the same command from the AUDIT section: trustchk -i -n tree / 2>&1 >/dev/null | grep untrusted Line by line, verify the root cause and act (one of): remove the offending object remove SUID/SGID settings remove privcmds setting add to TSD aka AllowList

title: Ensure world writable directories have the SVTX bit set
description: The system is audited for world writable directories. World writable directories are considered as a common application component - usually a location for temporary files. An audit should be performed on the system to search for the presence of world writable directories. Audit: automated read-only check derived from the CIS audit procedure; it prints "compliant" when the control is met.
reference: CIS IBM AIX 7 Benchmark v1.2.0 - 3.2 Ensure world writable directories have the SVTX bit set

audit.command: command -v find >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1; out=$( { find / \( -fstype jfs -o -fstype jfs2 \) -type d -perm -o+w ! -perm -1000 -ls ; } 2>/dev/null ); [ -z "$out" ] && echo compliant || printf '%s\n' "$out" | head -n 20

remediation.command: Review the local mounted JFS/JFS2 filesystems using the following command to find all world writable directories missing the SVTX bit: find / \( -fstype jfs -o -fstype jfs2 \) -type d -perm -o+w ! -perm -1000 -ls If a directory must retain world writable access, ensure that SVTX bit is set so that users can only remove the filenames they own: chmod o+t ${dir} NOTE: This will leave existing modes while adding the SVTX (also known as sticky bit) to the directory. The documented meaning of the flag for directories is: Sets the link permission to directories. Otherwise, remove world-write permission - without modifying the other mode bits: chmod o-w ${dir}

title: Ensure world writable files are secured
description: The system is audited for world writable files. An audit should be performed on the system to search for the presence of world writable files. In an extreme case - where this permission is required - the file needs to be added to the TSD and audit configurations. The preference is no world writeable files. Audit: automated read-only check derived from the CIS audit procedure; it prints "compliant" when the control is met.
reference: CIS IBM AIX 7 Benchmark v1.2.0 - 3.4 Ensure world writable files are secured

audit.command: command -v find >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1; out=$( { find / \( -fstype jfs -o -fstype jfs2 \) -type f -perm -o+w -ls ; } 2>/dev/null ); [ -z "$out" ] && echo compliant || printf '%s\n' "$out" | head -n 20

remediation.command: Run the following command to remove the write bit from other: find / \( -fstype jfs -o -fstype jfs2 \) -type f -perm -o+w -exec chmod o-w {} +

title: Ensure access on root user smit.log is configured
description: The smit.log file int the HOME directory of root maintains a history of all smit commands run as root. The smit.log file may contain sensitive information regarding system configuration, which may be of interest to an attacker. This log file must be secured from unauthorized access and modifications. Audit: automated read-only check derived from the CIS audit procedure; it prints "compliant" when the control is met.
reference: CIS IBM AIX 7 Benchmark v1.2.0 - 4.1.1.1 Ensure access on root user smit.log is configured

audit.command: command -v lsuser >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1; h=$(lsuser -a home root 2>/dev/null | sed -n "s/.*home=//p"); [ -n "$h" ] || exit 1; r=compliant; for f in "${h%/}/smit.log"; do if [ -e "$f" ]; then set -- $(ls -ld "$f"); s=$(printf '%s %s %s\n' "$1" "$3" "$4" | awk -v m='rw-r-----' -v o='' -v g='' '{ok=1; for(i=1;i<=9;i++) if(substr(m,i,1)=="-" && substr($1,i+1,1)!="-") ok=0; if(o!="" && $2 !~ ("^(" o ")$")) ok=0; if(g!="" && $3 !~ ("^(" g ")$")) ok=0; print (ok ? "ok" : $0)}'); [ "$s" = ok ] || r="$f: $s"; else :; fi; done; echo "$r"

remediation.guidance: Remove world read and write access to the root user's smit.log: HOME=~root if (test ${HOME} != "/") then HOME=${HOME}/ fi chmod u=rw,g=r,o-rwx ${HOME}smit.log chown root:system ${HOME}smit.log

title: Ensure SUID and SGID files are reviewed
description: The system is audited for both suid and sgid files and programs. An audit should be performed on the system to search for the presence of both suid and sgid files and programs. In order to prevent these files from being potentially exploited the suid and sgid permissions should be removed wherever possible.
reference: CIS IBM AIX 7 Benchmark v1.2.0 - 4.1.1.19 Ensure SUID and SGID files are reviewed

audit.command: Re-execute the appropriate find command and review the output. This should reflect the changes made in the remediation section. If there are non-local filesystems which cannot be un-mounted, use the following to find all suid and sgid files on local JFS/JFS2 filesystems only: find / \( -fstype jfs -o -fstype jfs2 \) \( -perm -04000 -o -perm -02000 \) - type f -ls If all non-local filesystems are un-mounted: find / \( -perm -04000 -o -perm -02000 \) -type f -ls

remediation.command: Review the currently mounted filesystems: mount Un-mount all non-local filesystems and cdrom media: unmount <mount point> If there are non-local filesystems which cannot be un-mounted, use the following to find all suid and sgid files on local JFS/JFS2 filesystems only: find / \( -fstype jfs -o -fstype jfs2 \) \( -perm -04000 -o -perm -02000 \) - type f -ls If all non-local filesystems have been un-mounted: find / \( -perm -04000 -o -perm -02000 \) -type f -ls Review the files and where possible, use the chmod command to remove the appropriate suid or sgid bits: chmod u-s <file> chmod g-s <file>

title: Ensure HOME directories are owned by root or the UID specified in /etc/passwd
description: All user home directories must have a suitable owner UID. The recommendation is to lock accounts when the HOME directory is not owned by the user or by root. This recommendation may be overruled by a site-specific policy statement. When the account is the owner - the security policy must specify that (some) accounts may have DAC authorization to modify HOME directory contents. Audit: automated read-only check derived from the CIS audit procedure; it prints "compliant" when the control is met.
reference: CIS IBM AIX 7 Benchmark v1.2.0 - 4.1.2.2 Ensure HOME directories are owned by root or the UID specified in /etc/passwd

audit.command: command -v lsuser >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1; out=$( { lsuser -R files -a id home account_locked ALL | while read name ids homes locks rest; do uid=${ids#id=}; home=${homes#home=}; locked=${locks#account_locked=}; [ "$uid" -ge 200 ] 2>/dev/null || continue; [ "$home" = /dev/null ] && continue; [ "$locked" = true ] && continue; if [ ! -d "$home" ]; then echo "$home does not exist ($name)"; continue; fi; o=$(ls -ld "$home/" | awk '{print $3}'); [ "$o" = "$name" ] || [ "$o" = root ] || echo "$name does not own $home ($o)"; done ; } 2>/dev/null ); [ -z "$out" ] && echo compliant || printf '%s\n' "$out" | head -n 20

remediation.command: Review the file(s) returned by the audit procedure and perform one of the following: Change the ownership of the <HOME_DIRECTORY> to the appropriate user. e.g. chown <USER> <HOME_DIRECTORY>. Lock the account incorrectly associated with the <HOME_DIRECTORY>. Delete the <HOME_DIRECTORY>. WARNING This will remove the directory and all files contained in the directory from the system. The following script may be used to lock the account referring to the <HOME_DIRECTORY>: For all local accounts with UID >= 200: #!/usr/bin/ksh -e # Provided to CIS by AIXTools # Copyright AIXTools, 2022 lsuser -R files -a id home account_locked ALL | while read name ids homes locks rest; do uid=$(echo ${ids} | cut -f2 -d =) if [[ ${uid} -ge 200 ]]; then home=$(echo ${homes} | cut -f2 -d =) locked=$(echo ${locks} | cut -f2 -d =) if [[ ${home} == "/dev/null" || ${locked} == "true" ]]; then continue elif [[ ! -d ${home} ]]; then /usr/bin/printf "%-32s does not exist; Run appropriate CIS remediation\n" ${home} ${name} continue else /usr/bin/perl -e ' $user=$ARGV[0]; $hd=$ARGV[1]; $uid=$ARGV[2]; $huid=((stat $hd)[4]); if ($huid != $uid && $huid != 0) { printf("Locked Account: %s ... (see CIS section 4.1.2.2)

title: Ensure all directories in root PATH access are configured
description: To secure the root users executable PATH, all directories must not be group and world writable. There should not be group or world writable directories in the root user's executable path. This may allow an attacker to gain super user access by forcing an administrator operating as root to execute a Trojan horse program. Audit: every directory in root's login PATH must be absolute, exist, be owned by root or bin and not be group/world writable.
reference: CIS IBM AIX 7 Benchmark v1.2.0 - 4.1.2.10 Ensure all directories in root PATH access are configured

audit.command: p=$(su - root -c 'echo $PATH' 2>/dev/null | tail -n 1); [ -n "$p" ] || exit 1; r=compliant; IFS=:; set -- $p; unset IFS; for d in "$@"; do case "$d" in "") r="empty entry (current directory) in PATH";; /*) if [ -d "$d" ]; then s=$(ls -ld "$d/" | awk 'substr($1,6,1)=="w" || substr($1,9,1)=="w" || ($3!="root" && $3!="bin") {print $1, $3}'); [ -z "$s" ] || r="$d: $s"; else r="non-existent directory $d in PATH"; fi;; *) r="relative directory $d in PATH";; esac; done; echo "$r"

remediation.command: Search and report on group or world writable directories in root's PATH. The command must be run as the root user. Directories which are group and/or world writable are marked with "WARNING" To manually change permissions on the directories: To remove group writable access: chmod g-w <dir name> To remove world writable access: chmod o-w <dir name> To remove both group and world ... (see CIS section 4.1.2.10)

title: Ensure root user has a dedicated home directory
description: The root user must have a dedicated home directory and not use / as their home directory. By default, the home directory for the root user on AIX is /. This means that all configuration files and directories it creates are visible to all users and may be accessible if the root user has a weak umask setting. Audit: automated read-only check derived from the CIS audit procedure; it prints "compliant" when the control is met.
reference: CIS IBM AIX 7 Benchmark v1.2.0 - 4.1.2.11 Ensure root user has a dedicated home directory

audit.command: command -v lsuser >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1; out=$(lsuser -a home root 2>/dev/null) || exit 1; [ -n "$out" ] && [ "$out" != "root home=/" ] && echo compliant || echo "$out"

remediation.command: Create a new home directory for the root user mkdir /root Set ownership and permissions on this directory chown root:system /root chmod 0700 /root Update the home directory for the root user chuser home=/root root Move any necessary configuration files or directories to this new directory

title: Ensure NIS client is not installed
description: The Network Information Service (NIS), formerly known as Yellow Pages, is a client- server directory service protocol used to distribute system configuration files. The NIS client was used to bind a machine to an NIS server and receive the distributed configuration files. The NIS service is inherently an insecure system that has been vulnerable to DOS attacks, buffer overflows and has poor authentication for querying NIS maps. NIS generally has been replaced by such protocols as Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP). Audit: automated read-only check derived from the CIS audit procedure; it prints "compliant" when the control is met.
reference: CIS IBM AIX 7 Benchmark v1.2.0 - 4.2.1 Ensure NIS client is not installed

audit.command: command -v lslpp >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1; lslpp -L >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1; out=$( { lslpp -L | grep -i 'bos.net.nis.client' ; } 2>/dev/null ); [ -z "$out" ] && echo compliant || printf '%s\n' "$out" | head -n 20

remediation.guidance: Ensure that all of the NIS daemons are inactive: stopsrc -g yp De-install the NIS client software: installp -u bos.net.nis.client

title: Ensure NIS server services are not in use
description: A Network Information Service (NIS) server is a host that provides configuration information to other hosts on a network. NIS servers store tables of information about users, groups, and more. They also maintain a set of maps and run the ypserv daemon, which processes requests from clients for information in those maps. Audit: passes when bos.net.nis.server is not installed; if NIS server is approved, review /var/yp/securenets manually.
reference: CIS IBM AIX 7 Benchmark v1.2.0 - 4.2.2 Ensure NIS server services are not in use

audit.command: command -v lslpp >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1; lslpp -L >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1; out=$( { lslpp -L | grep -i 'bos.net.nis.server' ; } 2>/dev/null ); [ -z "$out" ] && echo compliant || printf '%s\n' "$out" | head -n 20

remediation.guidance: Ensure that all of the NIS daemons are inactive: stopsrc -g yp De-install the NIS server software: installp -u bos.net.nis.server - OR - - IF - the NIS server package is required as a dependency, or NIS must be used in the environment, and is approved by local site policy: Ensure that all of the NIS daemons are inactive: stopsrc -g yp De-install the NIS server software: installp -u bos.net.nis.server Create and secure the /var/yp/securenets file (if it does not already exist): touch /var/yp/securenets chmod u=rw,go= /var/yp/securenets chown root:system /var/yp/securenets Edit the file: vi /var/yp/securenets Add the allowed subnets: 255.255.255.0 128.311.10.0 NOTE: The format of the file is netmask netaddr as shown in the example above. Explicitly define all valid network subnets (one entry per line). Stop and start NIS to implement the configuration changes: stopsrc -g yp startsrc -g yp

title: Ensure legacy NIS markers are removed
description: If NIS has been de-installed in the environment, or has historically been used, ensure the + markers are removed from/etc/passwd and /etc/group. The + entries in /etc/passwd and /etc/group were used as markers to insert data from a NIS map. These entries may provide an avenue for attackers to gain privileged access on the system. The + entries must be deleted if they still exist. Audit: automated read-only check derived from the CIS audit procedure; it prints "compliant" when the control is met.
reference: CIS IBM AIX 7 Benchmark v1.2.0 - 4.2.3 Ensure legacy NIS markers are removed

audit.command: command -v grep >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1; out=$( { grep "^+" /etc/passwd /etc/group ; } 2>/dev/null ); [ -z "$out" ] && echo compliant || printf '%s\n' "$out" | head -n 20

remediation.command: Examine the /etc/passwd and /etc/group files: grep "^+" /etc/passwd /etc/group If the above command yields output, delete the + line: vi /etc/passwd vi /etc/group

title: Ensure all entries in /etc/hosts.equiv are removed
description: This process removes all entries from the /etc/hosts.equiv file. The /etc/hosts.equiv file can be used to circumvent normal login or change control procedures. The existence of this file, with the relevant entries, can allow remote user access to a system bypassing local user and password authentication. Audit: automated read-only check derived from the CIS audit procedure; it prints "compliant" when the control is met.
reference: CIS IBM AIX 7 Benchmark v1.2.0 - 4.2.4 Ensure all entries in /etc/hosts.equiv are removed

audit.command: command -v grep >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1; out=$( { grep -Ev "^[[:blank:]]*(#|$)" /etc/hosts.equiv ; } 2>/dev/null ); [ -z "$out" ] && echo compliant || printf '%s\n' "$out" | head -n 20

remediation.command: Remove all entries from the /etc/hosts.equiv file: sed '/^\s*$/d; s/^\(\s*[^#].*\)/#\1/' /etc/hosts.equiv > /etc/hosts.equiv.work mv hosts.equiv.work hosts.equiv chown root:system /etc/hosts.equiv chmod 644 /etc/hosts.equiv Note: the above command removes blank lines and comments out any non commented entries.

title: Ensure that host based authentication files are not present
description: This recommendation removes all instances of .rhosts, .shosts and .netrc files from the system. The .rhosts, .shosts and .netrc files can be used to circumvent normal login or change control procedures. The existence of such files, with the relevant entries, can allow remote user access to a system bypassing local user and password authentication. Audit: automated read-only check derived from the CIS audit procedure; it prints "compliant" when the control is met.
reference: CIS IBM AIX 7 Benchmark v1.2.0 - 4.2.5 Ensure that host based authentication files are not present

audit.command: command -v find >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1; out=$( { find / \( -fstype jfs -o -fstype jfs2 \) \( -name .netrc -o -name .rhosts -o -name .shosts \) -print ; } 2>/dev/null ); [ -z "$out" ] && echo compliant || printf '%s\n' "$out" | head -n 20

remediation.command: Remove the.rhosts and .netrc files from all user home directories: find / \( -fstype jfs -o -fstype jfs2 \) -name ".netrc" -exec rm {} \; find / \( -fstype jfs -o -fstype jfs2 \) -name ".rhosts" -exec rm {} \; find / \( -fstype jfs -o -fstype jfs2 \) -name ".shosts" -exec rm {} \;

title: Ensure ftpd daemon is not in use
description: This entry starts the ftpd daemon when required. This service is used for transferring files from/to a remote machine. The recommendation is that ftp is disabled and sftp is used as a replacement file and directory copying mechanism. This ftp service is used to transfer files from or to a remote machine. The username and passwords are passed over the network in clear text and therefore insecurely. Unless required the ftpd daemon should be disabled. Audit: `lssrc -s inetd -l` must not list the service (count 0).
reference: CIS IBM AIX 7 Benchmark v1.2.0 - 4.3.4.9 Ensure ftpd daemon is not in use

audit.command: command -v lssrc >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1; n=$(lssrc -s inetd -l 2>/dev/null | grep -v tftp | grep -c 'ftp'); echo "$n"

remediation.guidance: In /etc/inetd.conf, comment out the ftp entry: chsubserver -r inetd -C /etc/inetd.conf -d -v 'ftp' -p 'tcp6' refresh -s inetd

title: Ensure rlogin daemon is not in use
description: This entry starts the rlogin daemon when required. This service authenticates remote user logins. This login service is used to authenticate a remote user connection when logging in via the rlogin command. The username and password are passed over the network in clear text and therefore insecurely. Unless required the rlogin daemon will be disabled. Audit: `lssrc -s inetd -l` must not list the service (count 0).
reference: CIS IBM AIX 7 Benchmark v1.2.0 - 4.3.4.19 Ensure rlogin daemon is not in use

audit.command: command -v lssrc >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1; n=$(lssrc -s inetd -l 2>/dev/null | grep -c '^rlogin'); echo "$n"

remediation.guidance: In /etc/inetd.conf, comment out the rlogin entry and refresh the inetd process: # /usr/sbin/chsubserver -r inetd -C /etc/inetd.conf -d -v 'login' -p tcp6 # /usr/bin/lssrc -s inetd && refresh -s inetd

title: Ensure telnetd daemon is not in use
description: The recommendation is that telnet is disabled and OpenSSH is used as a replacement mechanism. This entry starts the telnetd daemon when required. This provides a protocol for command line access from a remote machine. The telnet protocol passes username and password in clear text over the network in clear text and therefore insecurely. This telnet service is used to service remote user connections. Audit: `lssrc -s inetd -l` must not list the service (count 0).
reference: CIS IBM AIX 7 Benchmark v1.2.0 - 4.3.4.28 Ensure telnetd daemon is not in use

audit.command: command -v lssrc >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1; n=$(lssrc -s inetd -l 2>/dev/null | grep -c 'telnet'); echo "$n"

remediation.guidance: In /etc/inetd.conf, comment out the telnet entry: chsubserver -r inetd -C /etc/inetd.conf -d -v 'telnet' -p 'tcp6' refresh -s inetd

title: Ensure tftpd daemon is not in use
description: This entry starts the tftp service when required. The tftp service allows remote systems to download or upload files to the tftp server without any authentication. It is therefore a service that should not run, unless needed. Audit: `lssrc -s inetd -l` must not list the service (count 0).
reference: CIS IBM AIX 7 Benchmark v1.2.0 - 4.3.4.29 Ensure tftpd daemon is not in use

audit.command: command -v lssrc >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1; n=$(lssrc -s inetd -l 2>/dev/null | grep -c '[[:blank:]]tftp'); echo "$n"

remediation.guidance: Use chsubserver to disable this service in /etc/inetd.conf: chsubserver -r inetd -C /etc/inetd.conf -d -v 'tftp' -p 'udp6' refresh -s inetd

title: Ensure NFS client mounts include nosuid and nodev options
description: When using NFS shares ensure that suid/sgid program execution and/or access to system devices via permissions set on any mounted NFS filesystem are disabled. Setting the nosuid and nodev options means that files on the NFS server cannot be used to gain privileged access on the client. Audit: automated read-only check derived from the CIS audit procedure; it prints "compliant" when the control is met.
reference: CIS IBM AIX 7 Benchmark v1.2.0 - 4.4.1.3 Ensure NFS client mounts include nosuid and nodev options

audit.command: command -v lsnfsmnt >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1; out=$( { lsnfsmnt -l | egrep -v "^Name" | grep -v nosuid; lsnfsmnt -l | egrep -v "^Name" | grep -v nodev ; } 2>/dev/null ); [ -z "$out" ] && echo compliant || printf '%s\n' "$out" | head -n 20

remediation.command: For each NFS mount, disable suid programs and device access. List the current NFS mounts: lsnfsmnt -l | /usr/bin/egrep -v "^Name" | /usr/bin/grep -v "nosuid" | while read remote server mntpnt rest; do chnfsmnt -d ${remote} -f ${mntpnt} -h ${server} -y -z done lsnfsmnt -l | /usr/bin/egrep -v "^Name" | /usr/bin/grep -v "nodev" | while read remote server mntpnt rest; do chnfsmnt -d ${remote} -f ${mntpnt} -h ${server} -y -z done NOTE: The NFS mount needs is re-mounted automatically by chnfsmnt. NOTE: The second loop might not do anything as both loops set both nosuid (-y) and nodev (-z)

title: Ensure access by root over nfs is disabled or blocked
description: For each NFS export, ensure that the anon aka root_squash option is set to -2 or -1. Each NFS export on the server should have the anon=-2 option set. With this (default) value root (euid==0) is seen as the account nobody. When anon=0 the remote root user has root access on the NFS mount. Audit: automated read-only check derived from the CIS audit procedure; it prints "compliant" when the control is met.
reference: CIS IBM AIX 7 Benchmark v1.2.0 - 4.4.1.6 Ensure access by root over nfs is disabled or blocked

audit.command: command -v lsnfsexp >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1; out=$( { lsnfsexp | grep -v "anon=-1" | grep anon= ; } 2>/dev/null ); [ -z "$out" ] && echo compliant || printf '%s\n' "$out" | head -n 20

remediation.command: To change this value for all failing NFS exported filesystems: lsnfsexp | grep -v 'anon=-1' | grep anon= | while read fs rest; do chnfsexp -d ${fs} -a -2 done The command chnfsexp re-exports the file or directory with the new settings active.

title: Ensure secure RPC authentication is enabled
description: To enhance server-client authentication ensure that the secure option is selected for every export. RPC is a protocol used by NFS to communicate requests between hosts. Secure NFS uses encryption (DES or Kerberos) to secure host authentication in RPC transactions. Audit: automated read-only check derived from the CIS audit procedure; it prints "compliant" when the control is met.
reference: CIS IBM AIX 7 Benchmark v1.2.0 - 4.4.1.7 Ensure secure RPC authentication is enabled

audit.command: command -v lsnfsexp >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1; out=$( { lsnfsexp | grep sec= | grep none; lsnfsexp | grep -v sec= ; } 2>/dev/null ); [ -z "$out" ] && echo compliant || printf '%s\n' "$out" | head -n 20

remediation.command: Use chnfsexp to change/validate this value for all NFS exported filesystems: chnfsexp -d <fs> -S <sec> The available security method options are: sys - UNIX authentication dh - DES authentication none - Use the anonymous ID if it has a value other than -1 krb5 - Kerberos. Authentication only krb5i - Kerberos. Authentication and integrity krb5p - Authentication, integrity, and privacy Once all exported filesystems have been successfully validated or changed, re-export the filesystems and directories to activate the new options: exportfs -a

title: Ensure File System Level encryption is enabled
description: When there is a requirement for file based encryption for unauthorized users for both live systems and encryption at rest the preferred mechanism is EFS - encrypted file systems. A security enhancement introduced with AIX 6.1 is Encrypted Filesystems (EFS). This technology enables an individual user to encrypt their own data within a jfs2 filesystem. Audit: checks the CLiC filesets required for EFS are installed; verify efsenable and encrypted filesystems manually.
reference: CIS IBM AIX 7 Benchmark v1.2.0 - 4.4.2.1 Ensure File System Level encryption is enabled

audit.command: command -v lslpp >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1; r=compliant; for p in clic.rte.includes clic.rte.kernext clic.rte.lib clic.rte.pkcs11; do lslpp -L $p >/dev/null 2>&1 || r="$p not installed"; done; echo "$r"

remediation.command: There are two pre-requisite requirements for EFS, it requires RBAC and the installation of the CLiC cryptographic fileset. The fileset is located on the expansion pack, shipped with the AIX media. Place the CLiC software into a convenient location, such as /tmp and install via: /usr/lib/instl/sm_inst installp_cmd -a -Q -d /tmp -f clic.rte -c -N -g -X -G -Y NOTE: If the software is not located in /tmp, reflect the actual location in the command above. Load the CLiC kernel extension: /usr/lib/methods/loadkclic As the EFS administrator, create the initial keystore. This is typically the root user: efsenable -a An EFS enabled filesystem can be created with the following command: chfs -v jfs2 -g <vg_name> -m <filesystem> -a size=<size> -a efs=yes To enable EFS for an existing filesystem: chfs -a efs=yes <filesystem> To encrypt a file, load your keystore via: efskeymgr -o ksh Then encrypt via: efsmgr -c AES_192_ECB -e <filename> To decrypt: efsmgr -d <filename> Further details regarding planning and implementation of EFS can be found within the IBM AIX 7.1 Infocentre: https://www.ibm.com/docs/en/aix/7.1?topic=system-efs-encrypted-file NOTE: The ... (see CIS section 4.4.2.1)

remediation.command:
set -u
export DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive
tma_pkg_remove() { for p in "$@"; do
  if command -v dnf >/dev/null 2>&1; then dnf -y remove "$p";
  elif command -v yum >/dev/null 2>&1; then yum -y remove "$p";
  elif command -v apt-get >/dev/null 2>&1; then apt-get -y purge "$p";
  elif command -v zypper >/dev/null 2>&1; then zypper -n remove "$p"; fi; done; }
tma_pkg_install() { for p in "$@"; do
  if command -v dnf >/dev/null 2>&1; then dnf -y install "$p";
  elif command -v yum >/dev/null 2>&1; then yum -y install "$p";
  elif command -v apt-get >/dev/null 2>&1; then apt-get -y install "$p";
  elif command -v zypper >/dev/null 2>&1; then zypper -n install "$p"; fi; done; }
tma_svc_off() { for u in "$@"; do systemctl stop "$u" 2>/dev/null; systemctl mask "$u" 2>/dev/null; done; return 0; }
tma_bk() { [ -e "$1" ] && [ ! -e "$1.tmaegis.bak" ] && cp -p "$1" "$1.tmaegis.bak"; return 0; }
# tma_setkv FILE KEY VALUE: KEY=VALUE, replacing any active KEY= line (file created if missing)
tma_setkv() {
  f=$1; k=$2; v=$3; t="$f.tma.$$"
  tma_bk "$f"
  { [ -f "$f" ] && grep -v "^[[:space:]]*$k[[:space:]]*=" "$f"; echo "$k=$v"; } > "$t" || { rm -f "$t"; return 1; }
  if [ -f "$f" ]; then cat "$t" > "$f"; else mv "$t" "$f"; fi
  rm -f "$t"; return 0
}
# tma_comment FILE ERE: comment out active lines matching ERE (backup first)
tma_comment() {
  f=$1; re=$2; [ -f "$f" ] || return 0
  grep -Eq "$re" "$f" || return 0
  tma_bk "$f"; t="$f.tma.$$"
  awk -v re="$re" '$0 ~ re && $0 !~ /^[[:space:]]*#/ { print "#TMAegis# " $0; next } { print }' "$f" > "$t" || { rm -f "$t"; return 1; }
  cat "$t" > "$f"; rm -f "$t"; return 0
}

title: Ensure root access to ftpd is disabled
description: This change adds the root user to the /etc/ftpusers file, which disables ftp for root. This change ensures that direct root ftp access is disabled. As detailed previously, ftp as a service should be disabled. If the service has to be enabled then this change must be implemented to ensure that remote root file transfer access is not enabled. Audit: pattern match on /etc/ftpusers as described in the CIS audit procedure.
reference: CIS IBM AIX 7 Benchmark v1.2.0 - 4.6.2.1 Ensure root access to ftpd is disabled

remediation.guidance: Add root to the /etc/ftpusers file: echo "root" >> /etc/ftpusers

title: Ensure ftpd umask is configured
description: The umask of the ftpd service should be set to at least 027 in order to prevent the FTP daemon process from creating world-accessable, group-writeable files by default. The umask of the ftpd service should be set to at least 027 in order to prevent the FTP daemon process from creating world-accessable and group-writeable files by default. Audit: when ftp is enabled in inetd.conf, ftpd must run with -u 027 (or stricter 077).
reference: CIS IBM AIX 7 Benchmark v1.2.0 - 4.6.2.3 Ensure ftpd umask is configured

audit.command: l=$(grep "^ftp[[:blank:]]" /etc/inetd.conf 2>/dev/null); if [ -n "$l" ]; then printf '%s\n' "$l" | grep -Eq -- "-u[[:blank:]]*0?(027|077)" && echo compliant || echo "$l"; else echo compliant; fi

remediation.command: Set the default umask of the ftp daemon: [[ $(grep -c "^ftp[[:blank:]]" /etc/inetd.conf) -gt 0 ]] && chsubserver -c -v ftp -p tcp "ftpd -l -u 027" && refresh -s inetd || RC=0 NOTE: The umask above restricts write permissions for both group and other. All access for other is removed.

title: Ensure /etc/shosts.equiv and /etc/rhosts.equiv are removed
description: The recommendation is to remove both the /etc/shosts.equiv and /etc/rhosts.equiv file. This is a consequence of the recommendation to not use HostbasedAuthentification. The recommendation is to not use HostbasedAuthentification unless there is a documented need already exists the logical consequence is to remove these files, if they exist, to lower the risk of accidental activation. Audit: automated read-only check derived from the CIS audit procedure; it prints "compliant" when the control is met.
reference: CIS IBM AIX 7 Benchmark v1.2.0 - 4.6.3.2 Ensure /etc/shosts.equiv and /etc/rhosts.equiv are removed

audit.command: command -v ls >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1; out=$( { ls /etc/shosts.equiv /etc/rhosts.equiv ; } 2>/dev/null ); [ -z "$out" ] && echo compliant || printf '%s\n' "$out" | head -n 20

remediation.command: Print (for review) and then remove the content of the /etc/[rs]hosts.equiv files: for file in /etc/[rs]hosts.equiv; do print "+++ ${file} +++" /usr/bin/cat -n ${file} /usr/bin/rm -f ${file} done

title: Ensure sftp-server arguments are configured
description: The sftp-server is started by the sshd server after authentication has been completed successfully. The process runs with the euid of the authenticated user. The sftp- server does not inherit the logging levels from sshd and they must be configured manually. SFTP provides several logging levels with varying amounts of verbosity. Audit: evaluates the effective configuration from `sshd -T` (Match blocks must be reviewed separately).
reference: CIS IBM AIX 7 Benchmark v1.2.0 - 4.6.3.3 Ensure sftp-server arguments are configured

audit.command: command -v sshd >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1; out=$(sshd -T 2>/dev/null) || exit 1; r=compliant; for p in '^subsystem[[:blank:]]+sftp[[:blank:]]+(/usr/sbin/sftp-server|internal-sftp)[[:blank:]]+-u[[:blank:]]+027[[:blank:]]+-f[[:blank:]]+AUTH[[:blank:]]+-l[[:blank:]]+(INFO|VERBOSE)[[:blank:]]*$'; do printf '%s\n' "$out" | grep -Eiq -- "$p" || r="not matched: $p"; done; echo "$r"

remediation.guidance: Edit the /etc/ssh/sshd_config and set the sftp arguments to one of the following: Subsystem sftp /usr/sbin/sftp-server -u 027 -f AUTH -l INFO - OR - Subsystem sftp /usr/sbin/sftp-server -u 027 -f AUTH -l VERBOSE - OR - Subsystem sftp internal-sftp -u 027 -f AUTH -l INFO - OR - Subsystem sftp internal-sftp -u 027 -f AUTH -l VERBOSE Re-cycle the sshd daemon to pick up the configuration changes: # /usr/bin/stopsrc -s sshd; /usr/bin/sleep 5; /usr/bin/startsrc -s sshd

title: Ensure sshd Ciphers are configured
description: This variable limits the ciphers that SSH can use during communication. Notes: Some organizations may have stricter requirements for approved ciphers. Ensure that ciphers used are in compliance with site policy. The only "strong" ciphers currently FIPS 140 compliant are: o aes256-gcm@openssh.com o aes128-gcm@openssh.com o aes256-ctr o aes192-ctr o aes128-ctr Audit: the effective `ciphers` list from `sshd -T` must not contain any weak algorithm listed by CIS.
reference: CIS IBM AIX 7 Benchmark v1.2.0 - 4.6.3.6 Ensure sshd Ciphers are configured

audit.command: command -v sshd >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1; out=$(sshd -T 2>/dev/null) || exit 1; line=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | grep -i '^ciphers '); [ -n "$line" ] || exit 1; printf '%s\n' "$line" | grep -Eiq -- '(^|[ ,])((3des|blowfish|cast128|aes(128|192|256))-cbc|arcfour(128|256)?|rijndael-cbc@lysator\.liu\.se)(,|$)' && echo "weak: $line" || echo compliant

remediation.guidance: Edit the /etc/ssh/sshd_config file and add/modify the Ciphers line to contain a comma separated list of the site unapproved (weak) Ciphers preceded with a -: Example: Ciphers -3des-cbc,aes128-cbc,aes192-cbc,aes256-cbc,chacha20- poly1305@openssh.com Re-cycle the sshd daemon to pick up the configuration changes: stopsrc -s sshd startsrc -s sshd

title: Ensure sshd HostbasedAuthentication is disabled
description: The HostbasedAuthentication parameter specifies if authentication is allowed through trusted hosts via the user of .rhosts, or /etc/hosts.equiv, along with successful public key client host authentication. Host-based authentication is a method to authenticate users (rather than requiring password or key-based authentication method). Used at a system level by OpenSSH requires the file /etc/shosts.equiv to contain a list of so-called trusted hosts. Audit: evaluates the effective configuration from `sshd -T` (Match blocks must be reviewed separately).
reference: CIS IBM AIX 7 Benchmark v1.2.0 - 4.6.3.7 Ensure sshd HostbasedAuthentication is disabled

audit.command: command -v sshd >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1; out=$(sshd -T 2>/dev/null) || exit 1; r=compliant; for p in '^hostbasedauthentication[[:blank:]]+no$'; do printf '%s\n' "$out" | grep -Eiq -- "$p" || r="not matched: $p"; done; echo "$r"

remediation.guidance: Edit the /etc/ssh/sshd_config file to set the parameter above any Match entries as follows: HostbasedAuthentication no Re-cycle the sshd daemon to pick up the configuration changes: stopsrc -s sshd startsrc -s sshd Note: First occurrence of a option takes precedence, Match set statements withstanding.

title: Ensure sshd IgnoreRhosts is enabled
description: The IgnoreRhosts parameter specifies that .rhosts and .shosts files will not be used in RhostsRSAAuthentication or HostbasedAuthentication. Setting this parameter forces users to enter a password or provide an SSH key when authenticating with SSH, rather than trusting the remote host. Audit: evaluates the effective configuration from `sshd -T` (Match blocks must be reviewed separately).
reference: CIS IBM AIX 7 Benchmark v1.2.0 - 4.6.3.8 Ensure sshd IgnoreRhosts is enabled

audit.command: command -v sshd >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1; out=$(sshd -T 2>/dev/null) || exit 1; r=compliant; for p in '^ignorerhosts[[:blank:]]+yes$'; do printf '%s\n' "$out" | grep -Eiq -- "$p" || r="not matched: $p"; done; echo "$r"

remediation.guidance: Edit the /etc/ssh/sshd_config file to set the parameter above any Match set entries as follows: IgnoreRhosts yes Re-cycle the sshd daemon to pick up the configuration changes: stopsrc -s sshd startsrc -s sshd Note: First occurrence of a option takes precedence, Match set statements withstanding.

title: Ensure sshd KexAlgorithms is configured
description: Key exchange is any method in cryptography by which cryptographic keys are exchanged between two parties, allowing use of a cryptographic algorithm. Key exchange methods that are considered weak should be removed. A key exchange method may be weak because too few bits are used, or the hashing algorithm is considered too weak. Using weak algorithms could expose connections to man-in-the- middle attacks Audit: the effective `kexalgorithms` list from `sshd -T` must not contain any weak algorithm listed by CIS.
reference: CIS IBM AIX 7 Benchmark v1.2.0 - 4.6.3.9 Ensure sshd KexAlgorithms is configured

audit.command: command -v sshd >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1; out=$(sshd -T 2>/dev/null) || exit 1; line=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | grep -i '^kexalgorithms '); [ -n "$line" ] || exit 1; printf '%s\n' "$line" | grep -Eiq -- '(^|[ ,])(diffie-hellman-group1-sha1|diffie-hellman-group14-sha1|diffie-hellman-group-exchange-sha1)(,|$)' && echo "weak: $line" || echo compliant

remediation.guidance: Edit the /etc/ssh/sshd_config file add/modify the KexAlgorithms line to contain a comma separated list of the site approved key exchange algorithms Example: KexAlgorithms curve25519-sha256,curve25519-sha256@libssh.org,diffie-hellman- group14-sha256,diffie-hellman-group16-sha512,diffie-hellman-group18- sha512,ecdh-sha2-nistp521,ecdh-sha2-nistp384,ecdh-sha2-nistp256,diffie- hellman-group-exchange-sha256

title: Ensure sshd MACs are configured
description: This variable limits the types of MAC algorithms that SSH can use during communication. Notes: Some organizations may have stricter requirements for approved MACs. Ensure that MACs used are in compliance with site policy. The only "strong" MACs currently FIPS 140 approved are: o HMAC-SHA1 o HMAC-SHA2-256 o HMAC-SHA2-384 o HMAC-SHA2-512 Audit: the effective `macs` list from `sshd -T` must not contain any weak algorithm listed by CIS.
reference: CIS IBM AIX 7 Benchmark v1.2.0 - 4.6.3.11 Ensure sshd MACs are configured

audit.command: command -v sshd >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1; out=$(sshd -T 2>/dev/null) || exit 1; line=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | grep -i '^macs '); [ -n "$line" ] || exit 1; printf '%s\n' "$line" | grep -Eiq -- '(^|[ ,])(hmac-md5|hmac-md5-96|hmac-ripemd160|hmac-sha1-96|umac-64@openssh\.com|hmac-md5-etm@openssh\.com|hmac-md5-96-etm@openssh\.com|hmac-ripemd160-etm@openssh\.com|hmac-sha1-96-etm@openssh\.com|umac-64-etm@openssh\.com|umac-128-etm@openssh\.com)(,|$)' && echo "weak: $line" || echo compliant

remediation.guidance: Edit the /etc/ssh/sshd_config file and add/modify the MACs line to contain a comma separated list of the site unapproved (weak) MACs preceded with a -: Example: MACs -hmac-md5,hmac-md5-96,hmac-ripemd160,hmac-sha1-96,umac- 64@openssh.com,hmac-md5-etm@openssh.com,hmac-md5-96-etm@openssh.com,hmac- ripemd160-etm@openssh.com,hmac-sha1-96-etm@openssh.com,umac-64- etm@openssh.com,umac-128-etm@openssh.com - IF - CVE-2023-48795 has not been reviewed and addressed, the following etm MACs should be added to the exclude list: hmac-sha1-etm@openssh.com,hmac-sha2-256- etm@openssh.com,hmac-sha2-512-etm@openssh.com Re-cycle the sshd daemon to pick up the configuration changes: stopsrc -s sshd startsrc -s sshd

title: Ensure sshd PermitRootLogin is configured
description: This recommendation disables direct root login via SSH using a password. To be absolutely certain direct login is disabled the recommendation requires this variable is set rather than rely on a default that might change after an update to SSH. The recommendation requires an edit of the file /etc/ssh/sshd_config file to disable direct root login. Audit: evaluates the effective configuration from `sshd -T` (Match blocks must be reviewed separately).
reference: CIS IBM AIX 7 Benchmark v1.2.0 - 4.6.3.14 Ensure sshd PermitRootLogin is configured

audit.command: command -v sshd >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1; out=$(sshd -T 2>/dev/null) || exit 1; r=compliant; for p in '^permitrootlogin[[:blank:]]+(no|prohibit-password|without-password|forced-commands-only)$'; do printf '%s\n' "$out" | grep -Eiq -- "$p" || r="not matched: $p"; done; echo "$r"

remediation.guidance: #!/usr/bin/ksh PREFERRED_SETTING="prohibit-password" umask 077 set $(/usr/bin/egrep "^PermitRootLogin" /etc/ssh/sshd_config) echo $? if [[ ! -z $1 ]]; then # Look for a setting and change to no if anything else if [[ $2 != ${PREFERRED_SETTING} ]]; then sed "s/^PermitRootLogin \{1\}[^ ]\{1,\}/PermitRootLogin ${PREFERRED_SETTING}/" /etc/ssh/sshd_config >/tmp/sshd_config.$$ fi else # Look for a comment and append sed "/^# \{0,\}PermitRootLogin/ a\^JPermitRootLogin ${PREFERRED_SETTING}/" /etc/ssh/sshd_config >/tmp/sshd_config.$$ fi if [[ -e /tmp/sshd_config.$$ ]]; then diff -u /tmp/sshd_config.$$ /etc/ssh/sshd_config rm /tmp/sshd_config.$$ elif # Verify setting is specified /usr/bin/egrep "^PermitRootLogin" /etc/ssh/sshd_config >>/dev/null if [[ $? -ne 0 ]]; then print "PermitRootLogin ${PREFERRED_SETTING}" >> /etc/ssh/sshd_config fi fi Re-cycle the sshd daemon to pick up the configuration changes: stopsrc -s sshd sleep 5 startsrc -s sshd

title: Ensure sshd PermitRootLogin is disabled
description: The PermitRootLogin parameter specifies if the root user can log in using SSH. The current default is prohibit-password. Disallowing root logins over SSH requires system admins to authenticate using their own individual account, then escalating to root. This limits opportunity for non- repudiation and provides a clear audit trail in the event of a security incident. Audit: evaluates the effective configuration from `sshd -T` (Match blocks must be reviewed separately).
reference: CIS IBM AIX 7 Benchmark v1.2.0 - 4.6.3.15 Ensure sshd PermitRootLogin is disabled

audit.command: command -v sshd >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1; out=$(sshd -T 2>/dev/null) || exit 1; r=compliant; for p in '^permitrootlogin[[:blank:]]+no$'; do printf '%s\n' "$out" | grep -Eiq -- "$p" || r="not matched: $p"; done; echo "$r"

remediation.guidance: #!/usr/bin/ksh PREFERRED_SETTING="no" umask 077 set $(/usr/bin/egrep "^PermitRootLogin" /etc/ssh/sshd_config) echo $? if [[ ! -z $1 ]]; then # Look for a setting and change to no if anything else if [[ $2 != ${PREFERRED_SETTING} ]]; then sed "s/^PermitRootLogin \{1\}[^ ]\{1,\}/PermitRootLogin ${PREFERRED_SETTING}/" /etc/ssh/sshd_config >/tmp/sshd_config.$$ fi else # Look for a comment and append sed "/^# \{0,\}PermitRootLogin/ a\^JPermitRootLogin ${PREFERRED_SETTING}/" /etc/ssh/sshd_config >/tmp/sshd_config.$$ fi if [[ -e /tmp/sshd_config.$$ ]]; then diff -u /tmp/sshd_config.$$ /etc/ssh/sshd_config rm /tmp/sshd_config.$$ elif # Verify setting is specified /usr/bin/egrep "^PermitRootLogin" /etc/ssh/sshd_config >>/dev/null if [[ $? -ne 0 ]]; then print "PermitRootLogin ${PREFERRED_SETTING}" >> /etc/ssh/sshd_config fi fi Re-cycle the sshd daemon to pick up the configuration changes: stopsrc -s sshd sleep 5 startsrc -s sshd

title: Ensure root access is controlled
description: Restricts access to root via su to members of a specific group. Direct login via console and/or remote login via telnet is blocked. For accountability, no direct access to root is allowed. The attributes here control access to root for programs other than OpenSSH. Setting the sugroups attribute to SUADMIN ensures that only members of the this group are able to su root. Audit: root must have login=false and rlogin=false, and su must be restricted by sugroups (not ALL).
reference: CIS IBM AIX 7 Benchmark v1.2.0 - 4.8.1 Ensure root access is controlled

audit.command: command -v lsuser >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1; out=$(lsuser -a login rlogin su sugroups root 2>/dev/null) || exit 1; r=compliant; case " $out " in *" login=true "*|*" rlogin=true "*) r="$out";; esac; case " $out " in *" su=false "*) ;; *" sugroups=ALL "*|*" sugroups= "*) r="$out";; esac; case "$out" in *sugroups=*) ;; *) r="$out";; esac; echo "$r"

remediation.command: In /etc/security/user, set the root stanza sugroups attribute to SUADMIN and ensure the login and rlogin attributes are set to false: lsgroup SUADMIN >/dev/null || mkgroup -a SUADMIN chuser login=false rlogin=false sugroups=SUADMIN root NOTE: For the remediation the setting of su is irrelevant.

title: Ensure root user default shell is ksh
description: Ensure that the shell for the root user is set to /usr/bin/ksh Although the bash shell is available there are administrative processes that require the root user to be configured with the ksh shell as its default shell. Audit: automated read-only check derived from the CIS audit procedure; it prints "compliant" when the control is met.
reference: CIS IBM AIX 7 Benchmark v1.2.0 - 4.8.2 Ensure root user default shell is ksh

audit.command: command -v lsuser >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1; lsuser -a shell root 2>/dev/null

remediation.command: Execute the following command chuser shell=/usr/bin/ksh root

title: Ensure root user path does not include current working directory
description: This change removes any "." or "::" entries from the root PATH. If a "." or "::" is present the current working directory is included in the search path. Any "." and "::" will be removed from the root PATH. This means that any harmful programs placed in common PATH locations, would never be automatically executed. All directories must be explicitly defined within the PATH variable. Audit: automated read-only check derived from the CIS audit procedure; it prints "compliant" when the control is met.
reference: CIS IBM AIX 7 Benchmark v1.2.0 - 4.8.5 Ensure root user path does not include current working directory

audit.command: p=$(su - root -c 'echo $PATH' 2>/dev/null | tail -n 1); [ -n "$p" ] || exit 1; out=$(printf '%s\n' "$p" | awk '/(^:)|(::)|(:$)|(^\.:)|(:\.:)|(:\.$)|(^\.$)/'); [ -z "$out" ] && echo compliant || echo "root PATH: $out"

remediation.command: Examine root's PATH to see if it contains any "." or "::" entries: su - root -c 'echo ${PATH}' |awk '/((:[ \t]*:)|(:[ \t]*$)|(^[ \t]*:)|(^.:)|(:.$)|(:.:))/' If the command above yields output, remove the "." and "::" entries from the relevant initialization files. The files to examine are dependant on the root users shell definition in /etc/passwd. Once the file or files have been identified remove the "." and "::" from the PATH variable vi <filename>

title: Ensure all local user accounts have a hashed password
description: All (unlocked) accounts on the server must have a password. For this recommendation we look at the so-called files registery - as we cannot reliably review the entries kept in a centralized authentication system such as LDAP or Kerberos. An account password is a secret code word that must be entered to gain access to the account. If an account exists that has a blank password, multiple users may access the account without authentication and leave a weak audit trail. Audit: automated read-only check derived from the CIS audit procedure; it prints "compliant" when the control is met.
reference: CIS IBM AIX 7 Benchmark v1.2.0 - 5.1.1 Ensure all local user accounts have a hashed password

audit.command: command -v awk >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1; [ -r /etc/security/passwd ] || exit 1; out=$( { awk '/^[^ \t*].*:[ \t]*$/ {u=$1} /^[ \t]*password[ \t]*=[ \t]*$/ {print "Account " u " has a blank password"}' /etc/security/passwd ; } 2>/dev/null ); [ -z "$out" ] && echo compliant || printf '%s\n' "$out" | head -n 20

remediation.command: Check for accounts with an empty password field. If any, lock the account and assign an impossible password hash, as well as flag admin change (ADMCHG) to the password record. for user in $(/usr/bin/egrep -p "password = +$" /etc/security/passwd | awk '/:/ {print $1;}') do print "Locking account ${user} due to missing password" chuser account_locked='true' expires=0101000070 ${user} echo "$user:*" | chpasswd -e -f ADMCHG done

title: Ensure minimum password age is configured
description: The minimum password age determines the number of weeks that you must use a password before you can change it. Users may have favorite passwords that they like to use because they are easy to remember and they believe that their password choice is secure from compromise. Audit: reads `lssec -f /etc/security/user -s default -a minage`.
reference: CIS IBM AIX 7 Benchmark v1.2.0 - 5.2.2 Ensure minimum password age is configured

audit.command: command -v lssec >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1; out=$(lssec -f /etc/security/user -s default -a minage 2>/dev/null) || exit 1; v=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | sed -n 's/.*minage=\([^ ]*\).*/\1/p'); if [ -n "$v" ] && [ "$v" -ge 1 ]; then echo compliant; else echo "minage=$v"; fi

remediation.command: chsec -f /etc/security/user -s default -a minage=1

title: Ensure password history expiry is configured
description: The history expiry determines the number of weeks that a user will not be able to reuse a password. Users may have favourite passwords that they like to use because they are easy to remember and they believe that their password choice is secure from compromise. Audit: reads `lssec -f /etc/security/user -s default -a histexpire`.
reference: CIS IBM AIX 7 Benchmark v1.2.0 - 5.2.3 Ensure password history expiry is configured

audit.command: command -v lssec >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1; out=$(lssec -f /etc/security/user -s default -a histexpire 2>/dev/null) || exit 1; v=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | sed -n 's/.*histexpire=\([^ ]*\).*/\1/p'); if [ -n "$v" ] && [ "$v" -ge 52 ]; then echo compliant; else echo "histexpire=$v"; fi

remediation.command: chsec -f /etc/security/user -s default -a histexpire=52

title: Ensure passwords are controlled by password attributes
description: Ensure passwords are required to pass password attribute controls. If password restrictions are not enforced for some accounts, those accounts represent a much greater risk of being compromised by an attacker as they may have weaker passwords vulnerable to brute force attack or provide an indefinite window of opportunity ... Audit: automated read-only check derived from the CIS audit procedure; it prints "compliant" when the control is met.
reference: CIS IBM AIX 7 Benchmark v1.2.0 - 5.2.4 Ensure passwords are controlled by password attributes

audit.command: command -v grep >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1; [ -r /etc/security/passwd ] || exit 1; out=$( { grep NOCHECK /etc/security/passwd ; } 2>/dev/null ); [ -z "$out" ] && echo compliant || printf '%s\n' "$out" | head -n 20

remediation.command: In the file /etc/security/passwd clear the NOCHECK attribute from all users: #!/usr/bin/ksh -e # Copyright AIXTools, 2022 /usr/bin/grep -p NOCHECK /etc/security/passwd | /usr/bin/egrep ":$" | sed -e 's/://' | while read USER; do /usr/bin/pwdadm -c $USER /usr/bin/pwdadm -f ADMCHG $USER done

title: Ensure password expiration is configured
description: The maximum password age attribute (maxage) determines the maximum number of weeks that you can use a password before you must change it. The window of opportunity for an attacker to leverage compromised credentials or successfully compromise credentials via an online brute force attack is limited by the age of the password. Audit: reads `lssec -f /etc/security/user -s default -a maxage`.
reference: CIS IBM AIX 7 Benchmark v1.2.0 - 5.2.6 Ensure password expiration is configured

audit.command: command -v lssec >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1; out=$(lssec -f /etc/security/user -s default -a maxage 2>/dev/null) || exit 1; v=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | sed -n 's/.*maxage=\([^ ]*\).*/\1/p'); if [ -n "$v" ] && [ "$v" -ge 1 ] && [ "$v" -le 52 ]; then echo compliant; else echo "maxage=$v"; fi

remediation.command: chsec -f /etc/security/user -s default -a maxage=52

title: Ensure a strong password hashing algorithm is configured
description: The recommendation is to change the default password hash algorithm to ssha512 (see recommendation "Ensure pwd_algorithm is configured"). However, changing the default algorithm away from crypt is not enough. The user must supply a new password before a new hashed version of the password is stored in the shadow password file /etc/security/password. Audit: no stored password may still use a 13-character crypt hash in /etc/security/passwd.
reference: CIS IBM AIX 7 Benchmark v1.2.0 - 5.2.8 Ensure a strong password hashing algorithm is configured

audit.command: command -v grep >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1; [ -r /etc/security/passwd ] || exit 1; out=$( { grep -E "^[[:blank:]]*password[[:blank:]]*=[[:blank:]]*[^{*[:blank:]]{13}[[:blank:]]*$" /etc/security/passwd ; } 2>/dev/null ); [ -z "$out" ] && echo compliant || printf '%s\n' "$out" | head -n 20

remediation.command: Execute the following command to enable an administrative requirement to update password on next login - when current password is still hashed using the crypt algorithm. #!/usr/bin/ksh -e # hash_chk:5.2.12 # Provided to CIS by AIXTools # Copyright AIXTools, 2022 #SystemAccounts are skipped, root is treated a regular account #pconsole is no longer a system account - being deprecated/removed SACTS1="(adm|bin|daemon|invscout|ipsec|lp|lpd|nobody|nuucp|sshd|sys|uucp)" SACTS2="(esa|srvproxy|imnadm|anonymou|ftp)" grep 'password[[:blank:]]= .............$' /etc/security/passwd | \ while read pass equals cryptedhash; do user=$(/usr/bin/grep -p $cryptedhash /etc/security/passwd |\ /usr/bin/egrep -vp "${SACTS1}:$" |\ /usr/bin/egrep -vp "${SACTS2}:$" |\ /usr/bin/egrep '[a-zA-z0-9]+:$' | sed -e s/:$//) print ${user}: needs to update passwd set -x /usr/bin/pwdadm -c ${user} /usr/bin/pwdadm -f ADMCHG ${user} set +x done

title: Ensure minimum password length is configured
description: The minimum password length setting determines the lowers number of characters that make up a password for a user account. There are many different theories about how to determine the best password length for an organization, but perhaps "passphrase" is a better term than "password". The minlen option sets the minimum acceptable size for the new password. Audit: reads `lssec -f /etc/security/user -s default -a minlen`.
reference: CIS IBM AIX 7 Benchmark v1.2.0 - 5.2.9 Ensure minimum password length is configured

audit.command: command -v lssec >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1; out=$(lssec -f /etc/security/user -s default -a minlen 2>/dev/null) || exit 1; v=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | sed -n 's/.*minlen=\([^ ]*\).*/\1/p'); if [ -n "$v" ] && [ "$v" -ge 14 ]; then echo compliant; else echo "minlen=$v"; fi

remediation.command: chsec -f /etc/security/user -s default -a minlen=14

title: Ensure number of characters changed in new password is configured
description: The mindiff option sets the number of characters in a password that must not be present in the old password. Use of a complex password helps to increase the time and resources required to compromise the password. Password complexity, or strength, is a measure of the effectiveness of a password in resisting attempts at guessing and brute-force attacks. Audit: reads `lssec -f /etc/security/user -s default -a mindiff`.
reference: CIS IBM AIX 7 Benchmark v1.2.0 - 5.2.10 Ensure number of characters changed in new password is configured

audit.command: command -v lssec >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1; out=$(lssec -f /etc/security/user -s default -a mindiff 2>/dev/null) || exit 1; v=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | sed -n 's/.*mindiff=\([^ ]*\).*/\1/p'); if [ -n "$v" ] && [ "$v" -ge 6 ]; then echo compliant; else echo "mindiff=$v"; fi

remediation.command: chsec -f /etc/security/user -s default -a mindiff=6

title: Ensure password maximum repeated characters is configured
description: maxrepeats defines the maximum number of times a character may appear in a password. Use of a complex password helps to increase the time and resources required to compromise the password. Passwords which consist of too many repeated characters have lower complexity and thus are easier to compromise. Audit: reads `lssec -f /etc/security/user -s default -a maxrepeats`.
reference: CIS IBM AIX 7 Benchmark v1.2.0 - 5.2.13 Ensure password maximum repeated characters is configured

audit.command: command -v lssec >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1; out=$(lssec -f /etc/security/user -s default -a maxrepeats 2>/dev/null) || exit 1; v=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | sed -n 's/.*maxrepeats=\([^ ]*\).*/\1/p'); if [ -n "$v" ] && [ "$v" -ge 1 ] && [ "$v" -le 4 ]; then echo compliant; else echo "maxrepeats=$v"; fi

remediation.command: chsec -f /etc/security/user -s default -a maxrepeats=4

title: Ensure System Accounts cannot access system using ftp.
description: If ftp is active on the system, the file /etc/ftpusers is a deny list used by ftp daemon containing a list of users who are not allowed to access the system via ftp. The /etc/ftpusers file contains a list of users who are not allowed to access the system via ftp. All users with a UID less than 200 should typically be added into the file.
reference: CIS IBM AIX 7 Benchmark v1.2.0 - 5.3.10 Ensure System Accounts cannot access system using ftp.

audit.command: If ftp is active on the system, review the content of /etc/ftpusers and ensure there are no duplicate entries: cat /etc/ftpusers

remediation.command: List all users with a UID less than 200 to the /etc/ftpusers file: lsuser -c ALL | grep -v ^#name |grep -v root | cut -f1 -d: | while read NAME; do if [ `lsuser -f $NAME | grep id | cut -f2 -d=` -lt 200 ] > /dev/null 2>&1; then echo "Would add $NAME to /etc/ftpusers" fi done NOTE: Review the list of users Add all relevant users with a UID of less that 200 to the /etc/ftpusers file: lsuser -c ALL | grep -v ^#name |grep -v root | cut -f1 -d: | while read NAME; do if [ `lsuser -f $NAME | grep id | cut -f2 -d=` -lt 200 ] > /dev/null 2>&1; then echo $NAME >> /etc/ftpusers fi done

title: Ensure sudo is installed
description: The recommendation is to install and configure sudo, to reflect the privileged command access requirements of all users of the system. Privileged command access should be limited to and defined by a user's individual needs. Access to a root command prompt should limited, wherever possible, to minimize the risk of inadvertent or deliberate misuse of the account. Audit: sudo must be installed at version 1.9.17p1 or later.
reference: CIS IBM AIX 7 Benchmark v1.2.0 - 6.1.1 Ensure sudo is installed

audit.command: command -v sudo >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1; v=$(sudo -V 2>/dev/null | sed -n "1s/^Sudo version //p"); [ -n "$v" ] || exit 1; printf '%s\n' "$v" | awk -F"[.p]" '{a=$1*1000000+$2*10000+$3*100+($4==""?0:$4); print (a>=1091701 ? "compliant" : "sudo " $0 " is older than 1.9.17p1")}'

remediation.command: Install the latest available version for the sudo distribution installed on your system. This version should be 1.9.17p1 or later.

title: Ensure sudo logging is active
description: All commands executed via sudo should be logged to either syslog (default) or a dedicated log file Note: visudo edits the sudoers file in a safe fashion, analogous to vipw(8). visudo locks the sudoers file against multiple simultaneous edits, provides basic sanity checks, and checks or parse errors. Audit: automated read-only check derived from the CIS audit procedure; it prints "compliant" when the control is met.
reference: CIS IBM AIX 7 Benchmark v1.2.0 - 6.1.2 Ensure sudo logging is active

audit.command: c=$(cat /etc/sudoers /etc/sudoers.d/* 2>/dev/null); [ -n "$c" ] || exit 1; if printf '%s\n' "$c" | grep -Eiq "^[[:blank:]]*Defaults[[:blank:]]+logfile=[^[:blank:]]+"; then echo compliant; elif printf '%s\n' "$c" | grep -Eiq "^[[:blank:]]*Defaults[[:blank:]]+syslog_(bad|good)pri=none"; then echo "sudo syslog priority set to none"; else echo compliant; fi

remediation.command: Edit the file /etc/sudoers or a file in /etc/sudoers.d/ with /usr/sbin/visudo -f <PATH TO FILE> Remove any lines which are found containing: Defaults syslog_badpri=none -OR- Defaults syslog_goodpri=none -OR- If you do not want to log sudo commands to syslog, to use as sudo specific log file, edit the file /etc/sudoers or a file in /etc/sudoers.d/ with /usr/sbin/visudo -f <PATH TO FILE>: Defaults logfile="<PATH TO CUSTOM LOG FILE>" Example: Defaults logfile="/var/log/sudo.log"

title: Ensure sudo commands use pty
description: sudo can be configured to run only from a pseudo terminal (pseudo-pty) Attackers can run a malicious program using sudo, which would again fork a background process that remains even when the main program has finished executing. Audit: automated read-only check derived from the CIS audit procedure; it prints "compliant" when the control is met.
reference: CIS IBM AIX 7 Benchmark v1.2.0 - 6.1.3 Ensure sudo commands use pty

audit.command: c=$(cat /etc/sudoers /etc/sudoers.d/* 2>/dev/null); [ -n "$c" ] || exit 1; printf '%s\n' "$c" | grep -Eiq "^[[:blank:]]*Defaults[[:blank:]]+([^#]+,[[:blank:]]*)?!use_pty" && { echo "!use_pty set"; exit 0; }; printf '%s\n' "$c" | grep -Eiq "^[[:blank:]]*Defaults[[:blank:]]+([^#]+,[[:blank:]]*)?use_pty([[:blank:]]*,|[[:blank:]]*$|[[:blank:]]+#)" && echo compliant || echo "Defaults use_pty not set"

remediation.command: Edit the file /etc/sudoers with visudo or a file in /etc/sudoers.d/ with /usr/sbin/visudo -f <PATH TO FILE> and add the following line: Defaults use_pty Edit the file /etc/sudoers with visudo and any files in /etc/sudoers.d/ with /usr/sbin/visudo -f <PATH TO FILE> and and remove any occurrence of !use_pty

title: Ensure at is restricted to authorized users
description: at allows fairly complex time specifications, extending the POSIX.2 standard. It accepts times of the form HH:MM to run a job at a specific time of day. (If that time is already past, the next day is assumed.) You may also specify midnight, noon, or teatime (4pm) and you can have a time-of-day suffixed with AM or PM for running in the morning or the evening. Audit: at.deny must not exist and at.allow must exist (review its users).
reference: CIS IBM AIX 7 Benchmark v1.2.0 - 6.2.1 Ensure at is restricted to authorized users

audit.command: [ ! -e /var/adm/cron/at.deny ] && [ -f /var/adm/cron/at.allow ] && echo compliant || echo "at.deny present or at.allow missing"

remediation.guidance: Remove /var/adm/cron/at.deny if it exists: # /usr/bin/rm /var/adm/cron/at.deny IF /var/adm/cron/at.allow does not exist, create the file: # print "root\nadm" > /var/adm/cron/at.allow IF /var/adm/cron/at.allow already exists, ensure that it contains at least the root and adm users.

title: Ensure SSH client and server packages are installed on AIX 7.2
description: SSH client and server packages can be automatically installed as part of the base system to provide secure network login capabilities. On AIX 7.3 these packages are automatically installed on all systems, but on AIX 7.2 are an option. The telnet protocol is insecure and unencrypted. The use of an unencrypted transmission medium could allow an unauthorized user to steal credentials. The ssh protocol provides an encrypted session and stronger security. Audit: checks that openssh.base.server and openssh.base.client are installed (lslpp -L).
reference: CIS IBM AIX 7 Benchmark v1.2.0 - 1.3.3.2 Ensure SSH client and server packages are installed on AIX 7.2

audit.command: command -v lslpp >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1; r=compliant; for p in openssh.base.server openssh.base.client; do lslpp -L $p >/dev/null 2>&1 || r="$p not installed"; done; echo "$r"

remediation.command: Install the OpenSSH filesets from the AIX base media or IBM Web Download Pack: installp -acgXYd <media> openssh.base.client openssh.base.server

title: Ensure Secure by Default is selected during the installation
description: Secure By Default (SbD) is the concept of installing a minimal set of software in a secure configuration. The AIX Secure by Default (SbD) installation option installs a lighter version of the TCP client and server filesets, that excludes vulnerable commands and files. Many legacy services send passwords over the network in clear text and as such their use id discouraged.
reference: CIS IBM AIX 7 Benchmark v1.2.0 - 1.3.4.1 Ensure Secure by Default is selected during the installation

audit.command: Verify the configuration described in CIS IBM AIX 7 Benchmark v1.2.0 section 1.3.4.1: Secure By Default (SbD) is the concept of installing a minimal set of software in a secure configuration. The AIX Secure by Default (SbD) installation option installs a lighter version of the TCP client and server filesets, that excludes vulnerable commands and files.

remediation.command: The Secure by Default option can be found under option 3 of the Installation and Settings menu Installation and Settings Either type 0 and press Enter to install with current settings, or type the number of the setting you want to change and press Enter. 1 System Settings: Method of Installation.............New and Complete Overwrite Disk Where You Want to Install.....hdisk0 2 Primary Language Environment Settings (AFTER Install): Cultural Convention................English (United States) Language ..........................English (United States) Keyboard ..........................English (United States) Keyboard Type......................Default 3 Security Model.......................Default 4 More Options (Software install options) 5 Select Edition.......................standard >>> 0 Install with the current settings listed above. +----------------------------------------------------- 88 Help ? | WARNING: Base Operating System Installation will 99 Previous Menu | destroy or impair recovery of ALL data on the | destination disk hdisk0. >>> Choice [0]:

title: Ensure Allowlist violations are enabled
description: This takes allowlist aka whitelisting to the next level - where all software, libraries and scripts that are not in the trusted signature database (TSD) in /etc/security/tsd/tsd.dat are blocked. Trusted Execution (TE) provides an additional layer of access controls to processes on top of the base Discretionary Access Controls. Monitoring how processes access system resources can improve awareness of system integrity. Audit: automated read-only check derived from the CIS audit procedure; it prints "compliant" when the control is met.
reference: CIS IBM AIX 7 Benchmark v1.2.0 - 2.5 Ensure Allowlist violations are enabled

audit.command: command -v trustchk >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1; out=$(trustchk -p stop_untrustd stop_on_chkfail te 2>/dev/null) || exit 1; r=compliant; for p in '^STOP_UNTRUSTD=(ON|TROJAN)$' '^STOP_ON_CHKFAIL=ON$' '^TE=ON$'; do printf '%s\n' "$out" | grep -Eq -- "$p" || r="missing: $p"; done; echo "$r"

description: USER configuration files in their respective HOME directory e.g. $HOME/.profile, should only be accessible to the owner aka UID of the file. title: Ensure access on /audit and /etc/security/audit is configured
description: This recommendation verifies the access control settings for the default locations of AUDIT configuration and output files. The default location for the AUDIT subsystem configuration files are in /etc/security/audit. The default location for output produced by the audit subsystem is the firectory /audit. Access control must prevent unauthorized access. Audit: automated read-only check derived from the CIS audit procedure; it prints "compliant" when the control is met.

audit.command: command -v find >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1; out=$( { find /etc/security/audit /audit \( -perm -4 -o -perm -2 -o -perm -1 \) -o ! -user root -o ! -group audit ; } 2>/dev/null ); [ -z "$out" ] && echo compliant || printf '%s\n' "$out" | head -n 20

title: Ensure access to /etc/security is configured
description: The /etc/security directory contains multiple files and directories used to keep the targeted AIX system secure. Most subsystems are owned by root:security (UID:GID). However, additional systems such as AUDIT and AIXPERT have their own permissions (and recommendations). Traditionally, /etc/security has been identified as USER administration - including the shadow password file. Audit: automated read-only check derived from the CIS audit procedure; it prints "compliant" when the control is met.

audit.command: command -v find >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1; out=$( { find /etc/security -type d | egrep -v "security/(aixpert|audit|ice)" | sort | xargs ls -led | awk '{print $1 " " $3 " " $4 " " $9}' | egrep -v "dr[w-]x[r-]-[sS-]----" ; } 2>/dev/null ); [ -z "$out" ] && echo compliant || printf '%s\n' "$out" | head -n 20

remediation.command: Ensure correct access control settings for security subsystem configuration files installed in /etc/security: #!/usr/bin/ksh -e # Provided to CIS by AIXTools # Copyright AIXTools, 2022, 2025 EXCLUDE="security/(aixpert|audit|ice)" find /etc/security -type d | \ /usr/bin/egrep -v ${EXCLUDE} | \ /usr/bin/sort | xargs ls -led | \ /usr/bin/awk '{print $1 " " $3 " " $4 " " $9}' | \ /usr/bin/grep -v drwxr-s---- | \ awk '{print $NF}' | while read SECDIR; do /usr/bin/find ${SECDIR} | /usr/bin/grep -v ${EXCLUDE} | /usr/bin/xargs chown root:security /usr/bin/find ${SECDIR} -type d | /usr/bin/grep -v ${EXCLUDE} | /usr/bin/xargs chmod g-w+s,o-rwx /usr/bin/find ${SECDIR} -type f | /usr/bin/grep -v ${EXCLUDE} | /usr/bin/xargs chmod u-x,g-wx,o-rwx done

title: Ensure access on /var/adm/ras is configured
description: The /var/adm/ras directory contains log files which contain sensitive information such as login times and IP addresses. The log files in the /var/adm/ras directory can contain sensitive information such as login times and IP addresses, which may be altered by an attacker when removing traces of system access. title: Ensure access on /var/spool/cron/crontabs is configured
description: The /var/spool/cron/crontabs directory contains all of the crontabs for the users on the system. The /var/spool/cron/crontabs directory contains all of the crontabs for the users on the system. Crontab files present a security problem because they are run by the cron daemon, which runs with super user rights. Audit: automated read-only check derived from the CIS audit procedure; it prints "compliant" when the control is met.

description: The /var/spool/cron/atjobs directory contains scripts submitted by authorized users using the command at. title: Ensure legacy remote daemon support is not available
description: Ensure that software that supports passwordless and/or clear-text password connections is disabled. Examples include daemons such as: rlogind, rshd and talkd. Remote services that either send or receive usernames and passwords in clear text and should not be used. Audit: every file and directory of bos.net.tcp.rcmd_server / bos.net.tcp.rcmd must have mode 000 (or the filesets are absent).
reference: CIS IBM AIX 7 Benchmark v1.2.0 - 4.2.6 Ensure legacy remote daemon support is not available

audit.command: command -v lslpp >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1; out=$( { for fs in bos.net.tcp.rcmd_server bos.net.tcp.rcmd; do lslpp -L $fs >/dev/null 2>&1 || continue; lslpp -f $fs | grep -E "^ +/" | while read fn rest; do [ -L "$fn" ] && continue; if [ -d "$fn" ]; then ls -led "$fn" | grep -Ev "^d---------- "; elif [ -f "$fn" ]; then ls -led "$fn" | grep -Ev "^----------- "; fi; done; done ; } 2>/dev/null ); [ -z "$out" ] && echo compliant || printf '%s\n' "$out" | head -n 20

remediation.command: Use the following script to disable the files in these packages: Note: In this script, disable means chmod 0 ...; Remove any ACL; and update any entries in the TCB rather then remove entries. for fileset in bos.net.tcp.rcmd_server bos.net.tcp.rcmd do lslpp -L ${fileset} >/dev/null 2>&1 if [[ $? -eq 0 ]] then lslpp -f ${fileset} | /usr/bin/egrep "^ +\/" | while read command rest do # aclput will also do a classic chmod on the standard file mode bits /usr/bin/aclput </dev/null ${command} /usr/sbin/chtcb off ${command} # if in the TSD as a privileged command - make sure accessauths attribute is cleare lssecattr -c ${command} && setsecattr -c accessauths= ${command} # ignore errors, if any, when the file is not already in the TSD # Note: trustchk does not (always) update the attribute 'accessauths'. Ignore this if it occurs trustchk -u ${command} mode accessauths done # update the kernal security tables setkst fi done

title: Ensure writesrv service is not in use
description: The recommendation is to disable writesrv. title: Ensure snapp is not installed
description: snapp provides a perl-based interface to do the initial network configuration of an IBM RISC System/6000, from a Palm Pilot, via RS232C.
